questions.stem: In the R-T-M triangle, which side represents the target's own true movement over the plotting interval?
options: TM
RM
RT
The line from the centre to R
questions.explanation: RM is the target's movement relative to you, RT is your own run drawn from R, and TM is the target's true movement. Joining T to M removes your own motion from the relative plot.

questions.stem: Own speed is 15 knots. How long is the own-run line RT on a six-minute plot?
options: 2.5 nm
15 nm
1.5 nm
questions.explanation: In six minutes, one tenth of an hour, you steam one tenth of your hourly speed: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 nm.

questions.stem: On a six-minute plot, the line TM measures 0.8 nm. What is the target's true speed?
options: 0.8 knots
4.8 knots
8 knots
80 knots
questions.explanation: True speed is the length of TM for six minutes times 10: 0.8 × 10 = 8 knots.

questions.stem: On a head-up plot, TM points 100° from your heading line, and your course is 280°T. What is the target's true course?
questions.explanation: Target true course is the direction of TM relative to your heading plus your own course: 100 + 280 = 380, minus 360 = 020°T. Writing 380 or stopping at 100 are the usual slips.

questions.stem: Under Rule 19(d), what must a vessel that detects another by radar alone do?
options: Judge whether risk or close quarters is developing, and act in ample time
Sound five short blasts and wait for a reply
Hold course and speed until the other vessel is in sight
Stop and wait for the other vessel to give way
questions.explanation: Rule 19(d) requires the radar-only vessel to determine whether a close-quarters situation or risk of collision exists, and if so to take avoiding action in ample time. It does not tell you to hold on or to wait.

questions.stem: In restricted visibility, radar alone shows a target 30° on your starboard bow with risk of collision. Under Rule 19(d), which course alteration is to be avoided so far as possible?
options: An alteration to starboard
Any alteration larger than 10 degrees
Any alteration at all, so you must reduce speed instead
An alteration to port
questions.explanation: Rule 19(d)(i) says avoid an alteration to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than one being overtaken. A target 30° on the bow is forward of the beam. A starboard alteration is not prohibited and a bold one is what Rule 8 asks for.

questions.stem: A mate proposes a series of 5° course changes to avoid a ship detected by radar. What does Rule 8(b) say?
options: Several small alterations are preferred, as they are easier to steer
Alterations should never exceed 10° in restricted visibility
Make one large alteration that is readily apparent, not many small ones
The alteration must be exactly 90° to be seen on radar
questions.explanation: Rule 8(b) asks for a large, readily apparent alteration and warns against a succession of small ones, which another vessel cannot detect on radar.

questions.stem: Under Rule 19(e), a vessel cannot avoid a close-quarters situation with a vessel forward of her beam. What must she do?
options: Increase speed to clear the area quickly
Reduce to bare steerage way, stop if needed, and go with extreme caution
Alter course to port to pass astern of her
Stop only after the other vessel sounds a signal
questions.explanation: Rule 19(e) requires speed reduced to the minimum at which the vessel can be kept on her course, all way taken off if necessary, and extreme caution until danger of collision is over.

questions.stem: After altering course for a radar target, when can the vessel stop checking its effect?
options: Only when the other vessel is finally past and clear
As soon as the alteration is completed
After one more radar sweep
When the target's range begins to increase for the first time
questions.explanation: Rule 8(d) requires the effectiveness of the action to be carefully checked until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

questions.stem: A radar-only target is forward of your beam on the starboard bow. The plot shows CPA 0.8 nm. Using the worked example's figures, which choice best opens the CPA while following Rule 19(d)?
options: About 40° to port, which leaves the CPA about 0.8 nm
A 5° alteration to starboard, which the target cannot detect on radar
No action, because 0.8 nm is a safe passing distance in fog
A bold 40° alteration to starboard, opening the CPA to about 2.4 nm
questions.explanation: In the worked example a 40° starboard turn opens the CPA to about 2.4 nm, while a 40° port turn leaves it at about 0.8 nm and is the kind of move Rule 19(d)(i) warns against. A small turn is not readily apparent (Rule 8(b)). Whether 0.8 nm is acceptable is the master's judgement, and in fog it is usually too close.

questions.stem: On a plot, the point T lands exactly on M. What does that tell you about the target?
options: It is on a collision course
It is moving at twice your speed
It is stationary, such as a buoy or a moored boat
It is a false echo from own ship
questions.explanation: T is where a stationary object would have moved to because of your own motion. If T and M coincide, the target has no motion of its own.
